“It’s strange, but everyone who disappears is reported to have been seen in San Francisco. It must be a wonderful city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you think happened to Basil?” Dorian asked. He held his Burgundy up to the light and wondered how he could speak about it so calmly.

“I have absolutely no idea. If Basil wants to hide, that’s none of my business. If he’s dead, I don’t want to think about him. Death is the only thing that frightens me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked tiredly.

“Because,” Lord Henry said, holding the gold lattice of an open box of scented vinegar beneath his nose, “these days you can survive anything else. Death and vulgarity are the only facts in the nineteenth century that we cannot explain away. Let’s take our coffee into the music room, Dorian. You must play some Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house feels rather lonely without her. Of course, marriage is just a habit, and a bad one. But we miss even our worst habits when we lose them. Perhaps we miss those most. They are such an essential part of who we are.”

Dorian said nothing. He got up from the table, walked into the next room, and sat at the piano, letting his fingers wander over its white and black ivory keys. Once the coffee arrived, he stopped and looked across at Lord Henry. “Harry, have you ever thought that Basil might have been murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was very well liked, and he always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He wasn’t clever enough to make enemies. Of course, he had an extraordinary gift for painting. But a man can paint like Velasquez and still be terribly dull. Basil really was rather dull. He interested me only once. Years ago, he told me that he adored you passionately and that you were the main inspiration for his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” Dorian said, with sadness in his voice. “But aren’t people saying he was murdered?”

“Oh, a few newspapers are. It seems very unlikely to me. I know Paris has some dreadful places, but Basil wasn’t the sort of man who would visit them. He had no curiosity. That was his greatest fault.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you I had murdered Basil?” the younger man asked.

“But I wonder how long you would have carried on if you had been left alone. When would you have said anything if I hadn’t asked? My decision to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly made a difference. Too much of one, I’m afraid. What happens to the moral of our story if our happiness comes from breaking a promise? I should never have mentioned the subject. This simply won’t do.”

“You needn’t worry. The moral will be perfectly sound. Lady Catherine’s unjustifiable attempts to separate us cleared away all my doubts. I don’t owe my present happiness to your eagerness to express your gratitude. I was in no mood to wait for you to give me an opening. My aunt’s news had given me hope, and I was determined to find out everything at once.”

“Lady Catherine has been immensely useful, which should please her, since she loves to be useful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it only to ride over to Longbourn and feel embarrassed? Or were you hoping for something more serious?”

“My real purpose was to see you and try to judge whether I could ever hope to make you love me. My stated purpose, or the one I admitted to myself, was to see whether your sister still cared for Bingley and, if she did, to make the confession to him that I have since made.”

“Will you ever find the courage to tell Lady Catherine what awaits her?”

“I’m more likely to lack time than courage, Elizabeth. But it should be done, and if you give me a sheet of paper, I’ll do it immediately.”

“If I didn’t have a letter to write myself, I could sit beside you and admire your even handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I also have an aunt, and I mustn’t neglect her any longer.”

Reluctant to admit how greatly her closeness with Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had still not answered Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter. Now, however, she had news to share that she knew would be warmly welcomed. She felt almost ashamed to realize that her uncle and aunt had already missed three days of happiness, and immediately wrote the following:

“My dear aunt, I should have thanked you sooner for your long, kind, and thoroughly satisfying account of everything. To tell the truth, though, I was too annoyed to write. You imagined more than there really was. But now you may imagine as much as you like. Let your fancy run free, and let your imagination take every possible flight the subject allows. Unless you suppose me already married, you cannot go very far wrong.”

“Get up! What are you doing?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to work out where I was. The sun was already up, and I’d been fast asleep. Pap stood over me, looking both sick and angry. He said:

“What are you doing with that gun?”

I figured he didn’t remember anything he’d done, so I said:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“I tried, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t get you to move.”

“Well, all right. Don’t stand there talking all day. Get outside and see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll come along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I hurried out and up the riverbank. Bits of branches and other things were floating downstream, along with scattered pieces of bark. That told me the river was starting to rise. I thought what a fine time I could have if I were over in town. The rising water in June had always brought me luck. As soon as it began, firewood came floating down, along with broken sections of log rafts—sometimes a dozen logs together. All you had to do was catch them and sell them to the lumberyards and the sawmill.

I walked up the bank, keeping one eye out for Pap and the other on whatever the rising river might bring. All of a sudden a canoe appeared, a beauty about thirteen or fourteen feet long, floating high like a duck. I dived headfirst off the bank like a frog, with all my clothes on, and swam toward it. I half expected somebody to be lying inside. People often did that as a trick: they would wait until someone had rowed a little boat almost within reach, then sit up and laugh at him. But there was nobody this time. The canoe really had drifted loose. I climbed in and paddled it ashore. The old man will be pleased to see this, I thought. It’s worth ten dollars. But when I reached shore, Pap still wasn’t in sight. As I steered into a narrow little creek overhung with vines and willows, another idea came to me. I would hide the canoe carefully. Then, when I ran away, I could go about fifty miles downriver and camp in one place for good, instead of heading into the woods and wearing myself out walking.

I was quite close to the shack, and I kept thinking I heard the old man coming. Still, I managed to hide the canoe. Then I got out and peered around a clump of willows. There he was a little way down the path, taking aim at a bird with his gun.
